name: Grounds for Thought: Defence Colony
description: Grounds for Thought: Defence Colony, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Tuesday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.3rd September: Dr. Rahul KapoorWomen, Work and Well BeingWomen's participation in paid and unpaid work shapes far more than a household budget, it shapes physical, psychological, economic, and social well-being all at once. But that participation is rarely on equal terms: wage gaps, occupational segregation, invisible care work, and the daily balancing act between job and family all take a toll. Dr. Rahul Kapoor, Assistant Professor of Sociology and Social Work at Gautam Buddha University and author of Women and Work: The Sky is Full of Sexism, asks what a genuinely gender-sensitive approach to employment and social protection would actually look like — and why economic participation alone was never going to be enough.17th September: Anukriti AgarwalChacha Knows Best: Chacha Chaudhary and the Politics of NostalgiaBefore Indian households had cable or the internet, they had Chacha Chaudhary — a turbaned uncle whose brain worked faster than a computer, created by Pran Kumar Sharma in 1971. Fifty years on, that same deliberately ordinary uncle now sells toilets, water conservation, and voter turnout on behalf of government ministries. Anukriti Agarwal, a language educator and Fulbright Fellow at Yale, traces how a comic-book uncle went from newsprint to nation-building — and what it reveals when a state borrows the nostalgia the middle class grew up on.24th September: Dr Shashank SinghPrinces in the Polls: Indian Royals and Inherited Power in a Democratic Age, 1948–1967Between the 1950s and 60s, former princely elites didn't disappear from Indian politics — they reinvented themselves within it. Dr Shashank Singh, Junior Fellow at the Prime Ministers Museum and Library and a historian of Gwalior's princely order, uses electoral data and legislative debate from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh to show how monarchical charisma and patronage fused with electoral legitimacy. His argument: India's democratic consolidation didn't dismantle the feudal order so much as absorb and repurpose it.

For both of them you would have to write to us at workshops@museocamera.orgIs Cyanotype safe?Yes, cyanotype is one of the safest photographic processes out there.Meet your trainers Aditya AryaLead facilitator 45+ years of experience Photographer, historian and Founder-Director of Museo Camera with years of experience across advertising and fine art, he champions the slowness of analog processes. description: Grounds for Thought: Janpath, September 2026 A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Tuesday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.8th September: Prateek Mundeja Why Do Good Ideas Fail in Government? Governance is usually discussed in ideals — promises, ambition, the world as it ought to be. Prateek Mundeja, Assistant Professor of Political Science and Mookerjee Fellow (2025–26), argues that the more useful question is a duller one: what actually works? This session takes a realist's tour through limited resources, institutional capacity, and the gap between stated intentions and delivered outcomes — and makes the case that ideals only survive contact with the world when backed by hard, unglamorous choices.22nd September: Aarushee Shukla The Pause, The Buzzword, and The CollectiveIn a meeting room in Bihar and Kerala, Aarushee Shukla asked women what their collective meant to them, and got a long, deliberate silence back. That silence, she found, wasn't an absence of an answer — it was its own kind of answer, one we're rarely taught to read. This session recreates that pause live, then turns to the vocabulary — "empowerment," "participation," "social capital" — that runs through women's lives on paper, asking who gets to write those words and who is simply left to live inside them.29th September: Amitrajeet MukherjeeVoices from War: Revisiting John Keegan's The Face of BattleJohn Keegan's landmark book opened with a deceptively simple question — what is it actually like to be in a battle? Fifty years on, his witnesses remain almost entirely European, despite spanning centuries of warfare. Amitrajeet Mukherjee, a doctoral candidate in English Literature at Delhi University, widens that frame to the two and a half million Indians who served in the Second World War — diarists, letter-writers, the censored and the unrecorded — and asks whose voices get to define what "war writing" is for.
